strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: providing finite-sample guarantees for when LLM judge outputs can be trusted, which is timely given the growing use of LLM-as-a-judge in benchmarking and RLHF pipelines.

The methodology is technically coherent: the linearized expectation constraint (Eq. 5-6) with the largest-feasible-threshold rule is correctly adapted to pairwise judging, and the proof of Theorem 2.1 in Appendix A is complete, including the degenerate abstain-all case.

BPE is a simple, well-motivated uncertainty signal: averaging preference probabilities across both response orders to enforce permutation invariance, then applying binary entropy, is a natural way to disentangle genuine ambiguity from position-induced overconfidence at only 2 forward passes per instance.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: 3 benchmarks (MT-Bench, RewardBench, Chatbot Arena), 4 judge scales (7B to 70B), 5 risk levels, and results averaged over 1,000 random calibration/test splits with variance bands, which supports the claim that SCOPE tracks the target risk tightly (0.097-0.099 at alpha=0.10).
Baselines are sensibly chosen and include a strong, expensive competitor (simulated annotators from Jung et al., 2025), showing BPE achieves better AUROC/AUPRC at a fraction of the cost.
The limitations section is honest and specific (exchangeability assumption, white-box logit requirement, binary-only formulation, residual non-positional biases).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core statistical machinery is directly imported from Wang et al. (2025a) LEC and conformal risk control; the authors themselves note the proof follows 'the identical step in the single-model proof.' The contribution is essentially an application/adaptation of existing risk control to a new task, plus a simple heuristic (average two permuted probabilities, take entropy). BPE-style bidirectional evaluation and position-swap aggregation are well-known practices (Zheng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025d), so the novelty of both components is modest.

The 'FDR' terminology is misleading: the quantity controlled (Eq. 1) is the conditional error rate of selective classification, not a false discovery rate in the standard multiple-testing sense; this framing may overstate the connection to the FDR literature.

Practical utility is questionable at strict risk levels: on the hardest benchmark (MT-Bench at alpha=0.10), SCOPE coverage is only 0.246-0.543, and at alpha=0.05 coverage drops to 0.018-0.072 on MT-Bench. The headline 'up to 2.4x more judgments' abstracts over the fact that absolute coverage can be very low, limiting real-world usefulness of the guaranteed mode.

The uncertainty-quality improvements are mixed: Table 1 shows BPE sometimes has notably worse ECE than verbalized confidence (e.g., Qwen-14B MT-Bench 0.174 vs 0.114; Llama-70B MT-Bench 0.145 vs 0.096), so the abstract's claim that BPE 'improves uncertainty quality over standard confidence proxies' is only consistently true for discrimination (AUROC/AUPRC), not calibration.

The heuristic baseline description appears inconsistent: it is defined as accepting 'whenever the uncertainty score exceeds 1 - alpha,' but the BPE entropy score is bounded by 0.693, making the rule vacuous for alpha <= 0.3; the reported behavior suggests a confidence-based rule was actually used, and this should be clarified.

No code release or reproducibility artifact is mentioned, despite heavy reliance on exact prompt templates, logit-extraction details, and 1,000 seeded splits; the appendix helps but a code link would substantially strengthen reproducibility.

Correctness is defined as agreement with a single human label; human preferences can be noisy or genuinely ambiguous, and the paper does not discuss how label noise interacts with the risk guarantee (a 'wrong' judge verdict may reflect human label noise rather than judge error).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: providing finite-sample reliability guarantees for LLM-as-a-judge, where heuristic confidence thresholding is known to be unreliable due to position bias and miscalibration.

The framing is clean: selective pairwise judging with an accepted-set error bound (FDR ≤ α), and the empirical results over 1,000 random calibration/test splits consistently show empirical risk just below the target (0.097–0.099 at α = 0.10) across three benchmarks and four judge scales, which is what the theory predicts.
The proof of Theorem 2.1 (Appendix A) is complete and correct: the exchangeability step and the linearized-loss bounding argument are valid, and the degenerate case (empty feasible set) is handled.

Experimental hygiene is generally good: prompt templates, logit extraction details, baseline configurations (verbalized confidence, simulated annotators), hardware, and seeding are documented in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
The limitations section is honest and specific (exchangeability assumption, two forward passes for BPE, white-box logit requirement, binary-only formulation, residual non-positional biases).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core calibration machinery is a direct application of linear expectation constraints (Wang et al., 2025a) and conformal risk control (Angelopoulos et al., 2024) to pairwise judging — the proof even states 'See Wang et al. (2025a) for the identical step.' BPE is essentially the standard position-swap-and-average debiasing heuristic (Zheng et al., 2023) plus a binary entropy transform, so both contributions are incremental recombinations of existing tools.

A critical ablation is missing. The naive baseline uses predictive probability as its score (footnote 1), so SCOPE's reported coverage gains confound two factors: the better BPE uncertainty signal and the finite-sample calibration correction. Running naive calibration with the BPE score would isolate the contribution of the calibration procedure itself, but this experiment is absent.

Dataset construction is unclear and possibly problematic: the paper claims to randomly sample N = 2,000 non-tied instances from MT-Bench, yet MT-Bench contains only 80 questions × 2 turns ≈ 160 comparisons. Where the 2,000 pairwise instances come from (cross-model pair generation? GPT-4-generated pairs?) is never explained, undermining reproducibility and raising questions about what 'ground-truth human preferences' means on this benchmark.

The guarantee is marginal over calibration-set randomness, but parts of the text ('maintains a guaranteed error rate across the distribution of queries', 'test-time conditional error') could be read as implying per-instance or conditional guarantees, which the theory does not provide. This should be stated more carefully.

The heuristic baseline is ambiguously or incorrectly specified: 'accepts predictions whenever the uncertainty score exceeds 1 − α' would accept nothing for entropy scores bounded by 0.693 (or everything, contradicting the reported coverage of 0.809–0.958). The baseline description appears to conflate uncertainty and confidence, weakening the claimed comparison.

Uncertainty-quality results are mixed: BPE does not consistently improve ECE (e.g., worse than verbalized confidence for Qwen-14B and Llama-70B on MT-Bench, and worse than predictive probability on several configurations), so the abstract's claim that BPE 'improves uncertainty quality over standard confidence proxies' is stronger than the evidence.

The headline claim of 'up to 2.4× more judgments' rests on the weakest judge/dataset cell (Qwen-7B MT-Bench, coverage 0.246 vs 0.102); on stronger judges the gain over naive calibration is much smaller or marginal, and the practical value at such low coverage is debatable.
Figures 2's 3D bar charts are hard to read and obscure the risk–coverage tradeoff; a standard coverage-vs-α line plot per model would communicate the results better.
No code release is mentioned, and given the nonstandard data construction on MT-Bench, independent verification of the empirical results would be difficult.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem: providing statistical reliability guarantees for LLM-as-a-judge pipelines, which are increasingly used in benchmarking and RLHF-style training loops.

The core framework is technically sound: Theorem 2.1's proof (Appendix A) correctly adapts the linear expectation constraint (LEC) argument of Wang et al. (2025a) to the binary pairwise judging setting, and the 'largest feasible threshold' rule in Eq. 6 preserves validity since any threshold satisfying the calibration constraint inherits the guarantee.

BPE is a sensible, lightweight uncertainty signal: querying both response orderings and aggregating preference probabilities is a direct way to enforce permutation invariance at a cost of only two forward passes, in contrast to expensive multi-sample approaches like simulated annotators.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: three benchmarks, four judge scales, five risk levels, and 1,000 random calibration/test splits with variance bands (Figure 3), which is the right protocol for verifying a marginal finite-sample guarantee. The observed risk (0.097-0.099 at alpha=0.10) confirms the guarantee is not vacuous and not overly conservative.
The limitations section is honest and substantive, correctly identifying exchangeability fragility, white-box logit requirements, the binary-judgment restriction, and residual non-positional biases.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The finite-sample guarantee is a direct transplant of LEC (Wang et al., 2025a) with a straightforward proof, and BPE reduces to averaging two softmax probabilities and taking binary entropy. The contribution is essentially a careful application/instantiation to pairwise judging rather than a new method or new theory.

The headline claim ('accepts up to 2.4x more judgments') is only established against weak baselines: vanilla prediction, heuristic thresholding, and naive empirical calibration. No end-to-end comparison is made against other provably risk-controlled selective prediction methods (e.g., the Clopper-Pearson and fixed-sequence-testing baselines the introduction criticizes for sacrificing coverage, COIN of Wang et al. 2025b, or Jung et al. 2025's trust-or-escalate framework, which is cited and used only as an uncertainty baseline). Without these comparisons, the central advantage claim over existing guaranteed methods is not fully supported.

The heuristic-thresholding baseline appears mis-specified or strawman: it is described as accepting predictions 'whenever the uncertainty score exceeds 1 - alpha', which is backwards for an uncertainty score (high uncertainty should trigger abstention). The reported behavior (high coverage ~0.9 with risk ~0.25) is consistent with a broken rule, inflating SCOPE's relative advantage.

Verbalized confidence results look degenerate (AUROC ~0.45-0.50 across all settings, worse than chance-adjacent), suggesting the baseline may be under-implemented (e.g., parsing or prompt-formatting issues) rather than genuinely this uninformative.

The uncertainty-quality results are mixed: BPE improves AUROC/AUPRC in most but not all settings, and its ECE is sometimes clearly worse (e.g., Llama-70B on MT-Bench: 0.145 vs. 0.096 for verbalized confidence). The paper acknowledges this but the narrative overstates consistency.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility despite detailed prompts and configurations in the appendix.

The exchangeability assumption is stated as a limitation but never stress-tested empirically (e.g., under distribution shift between calibration and test splits), which is the practically dominant failure mode for conformal guarantees in LLM evaluation.

strengths: The paper is technically solid: the finite-sample validity proof (Theorem 2.1, Appendix A) correctly adapts the linear expectation constraint machinery (Wang et al., 2025b) to selective pairwise judging, with the exchangeability argument and the -1 budget correction laid out cleanly, including the degenerate all-abstain case.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: 5 benchmarks (3 main + JudgeBench and PKU-SafeRLHF), 4 judge scales, 1,000 random calibration/test splits, and comparisons against closely related and nontrivial baselines (Swap-and-Aggregate, Simulated Annotators, Trust-or-Escalate, Self-Consistency), which is more than most papers in this space provide.

The empirical risk curves (Figures 3 and 7) convincingly demonstrate that SCOPE tracks the target alpha across risk levels and models rather than being valid only on average, and the ablations (label noise in Appendix F, calibration set size in G, cross-benchmark transfer in H) probe exactly the right failure modes, including an honest demonstration that the guarantee breaks under distribution shift.

The paper is transparent about limitations (exchangeability, two-pass cost, white-box logit requirement, binary-only formulation) and the limitations discussion is honest rather than defensive. Reproducibility details (prompts, logit extraction, seeds, hardware, dataset sampling protocol) are provided in the appendix.

The demonstration on Skywork-Critic (Appendix E), where verbalized confidence collapses to AUROC 0.5, is a genuinely informative result about the judge-dependence of uncertainty signals and supports the paper's motivation for probability-based bidirectional aggregation.
weaknesses: Limited originality of both components. SCOPE is a direct application of existing conformal risk control / linear expectation constraint methods to a new task, and the validity proof largely restates the argument of Wang et al. (2025b). BPE is a small variation on well-known position-bias mitigation (bidirectional querying plus softmax averaging plus binary entropy); the main novelty is the aggregation granularity (probability-level rather than vote-level).

A key ablation is missing: the paper does not report 'naive calibration + BPE score' (i.e., the same well-ranked uncertainty signal with empirical threshold tuning and no finite-sample correction). Without it, the headline coverage gains (up to 2.4x) conflate the contribution of the BPE score with that of the conformal calibration rule, and it is unclear how much of the improvement over the Naive baseline is attributable to the statistical machinery versus simply using a better score.

The 'FDR' terminology is a misnomer. There is no multiple-testing structure here; the controlled quantity is the error rate among accepted judgments (selective risk). Framing it as FDR borrows gravitas from multiple testing without the corresponding structure and could mislead readers.

Practical utility at strict risk levels is questionable: coverage at alpha = 0.10 is low in several regimes (0.246 for Qwen-7B on MT-Bench, 0.023 on JudgeBench, near-zero coverage at larger calibration noise), and the framework requires a fresh labeled calibration set drawn exchangeably from the deployment distribution, which the transfer experiment shows is essential. The 'drop-in, user-tunable knob' framing in the conclusion somewhat overstates the deployability given these constraints.

Ground-truth human preference labels are treated as noiseless for the guarantee, but the same appendix shows calibration is highly sensitive to label noise; the guarantee story and the calibration-label-quality requirement sit in some tension that is acknowledged only implicitly.

Some experimental choices reduce comparability: Simulated Annotators and Self-Consistency are restricted to subsets of models/judges for cost reasons, and the strong accuracy gains of SC (7-10 points) are dismissed because its vote-agreement confidence is poorly ranked - a fair point, but it means the strongest available judge configuration is never evaluated selectively.

strengths: The paper is technically solid: the finite-sample validity proof (Theorem 2.1, Appendix A) is carefully laid out, the exchangeability argument is correctly handled (BPE is a deterministic function of x, so exchangeability transfers to the induced tuples), and the linearized expectation constraint is a sound way to control the accepted-set error rate on finite samples.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: three main benchmarks (MT-Bench, RewardBench, Chatbot Arena) plus two extended ones (JudgeBench, PKU-SafeRLHF), four judges across scales, 1,000 random calibration/test splits, and useful ablations covering calibration label noise (App. F), calibration set size (App. G), and cross-benchmark transfer (App. H). The drop-in deployment on a specialized critic (Skywork-Critic, App. E) is a nice generalization check.

The paper is honest about failure modes: Table 12 transparently reports that cross-benchmark transfer violates the risk bound in one direction (risk up to 0.20), and the limitations section correctly identifies exchangeability, compute overhead, white-box requirements, and the pairwise-only scope.

The main claim of the paper — that baselines (vanilla, heuristic, naïve calibration) violate the α constraint while SCOPE tracks it (empirical risk 0.097–0.099 at α=0.10) — is convincingly demonstrated, and the coverage-vs-α curves (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) show the method uses the risk budget rather than abstaining excessively.
Clear writing overall, with a well-designed Figure 1 and an explicit protocol (50/50 splits, repeated randomization, logit extraction details) that supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited originality. Both components are close to existing work: the calibration machinery is a direct application of the linear expectation constraints of Wang et al. (2025b) (the proof in Appendix A explicitly reproduces their argument), and BPE is a small delta over Swap-and-Aggregate (Zheng et al., 2023) — averaging the swapped-pass probabilities instead of voting, then applying binary entropy. The paper's own Table 1 shows the accuracy is identical by construction, and the ECE/AUROC/AUPRC gains over S&A, while consistent, are modest in many cells (e.g., Llama-70B Arena AUROC 0.736 vs 0.720). The contribution is an application-level combination rather than a new statistical idea.

The headline 'up to 2.4× more judgments' (abstract) is against the naïve-calibration baseline, a weak strawman; against the more principled Trust-or-Escalate comparison (relegated to Appendix D.2, Table 7), the gains are 1.1–3.2× but only on MT-Bench. The strongest baseline comparisons being in the appendix weakens the main-text evidential picture.

Practical utility at strict risk levels is questionable: at α=0.10, coverage on MT-Bench is only 0.246–0.543, and on JudgeBench for Qwen-7B it collapses to 0.023 with a large std — meaning the framework accepts almost nothing in some realistic regimes. The paper does not discuss when selective judging is actually useful versus just returning the raw verdict.

The marginal-FDR guarantee is weaker than the 'FDR' framing suggests: it is an expectation over the joint randomness of the calibration set and test point (a data-pooling guarantee), not a per-deployment or conditional guarantee. A practitioner calibrating once on a fixed set can see realized accepted-set errors above α (visible as the wide ±1σ bands for Qwen-7B in Fig. 3). The text could be clearer about this distinction.

The label-noise experiment (App. F) shows risk *decreasing* as calibration noise grows with coverage collapsing toward zero at ε=15–20%. While described as the 'desirable failure mode', it also indicates that under realistic label noise (human preference agreement is well below 100%) the method may be too conservative to be useful; this trade-off is not analyzed.

Position-bias mitigation is claimed as a benefit of BPE, but the paper never directly measures position bias (e.g., agreement rate between forward and reverse passes, or per-instance bias decomposition); the claim that disagreement 'is a strong indicator of systematic bias rather than true confidence' is asserted intuitively rather than evidenced.

Verbalized confidence has AUROC at or below chance (0.45–0.50) across nearly all cells, which is a surprisingly degenerate result for a published baseline; some verification of the implementation/parsing (given known results that verbalized confidence is weak but generally above chance in ranking) would strengthen confidence in the comparisons.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—when to trust LLM judge decisions—with a clean selective-prediction abstraction and a user-specified risk knob, which is well motivated by documented judge failure modes (position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference).

The technical core is sound: the finite-sample calibration (Eq. 5–6) follows the linear expectation constraint framework (Wang et al., 2025b), and the appendix proof of Theorem 2.1 is essentially correct—the exchangeability swap argument and the −1 budget absorbing the worst-case test-point loss are both properly justified, including the degenerate all-abstain case.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: 4 judge models, 5 benchmarks (including reasoning-heavy JudgeBench and safety-focused PKU-SafeRLHF), 1,000 random calibration/test splits, comparison to a strong guaranteed baseline (Trust-or-Escalate), and useful ablations on calibration-label noise, calibration-set size, cross-benchmark transfer (honestly showing guarantee failure under shift), and drop-in deployment on a specialized critic (Skywork-Critic).

The BPE-vs-Swap-and-Aggregate comparison is well designed: since both share the bidirectional prediction rule, the gains in ECE/AUROC/AUPRC isolate the value of probability-level aggregation over discrete vote agreement, and the analysis of paired baselines sharing prediction rules is transparent.

Limitations are discussed honestly (exchangeability, 2× forward passes, white-box requirement, pairwise-only scope), and the cross-benchmark transfer experiment directly probes the exchangeability caveat rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the risk-control machinery is adopted from Wang et al. (2025b) (LEC) and Angelopoulos et al. (2024) with adaptation, and BPE is a small modification of the well-known swap-and-aggregate protocol (Zheng et al., 2023)—averaging bidirectional probabilities and applying binary entropy. The contribution is a sensible combination rather than a new technique or new theory; the proof closely mirrors the LEC proof.

The framing overstates the guarantee. The result is a marginal FDR bound in expectation over calibration and test randomness; Figure 3 and Table 5 show large per-split variance (e.g., risk std of 0.086 on JudgeBench), so on many individual calibration runs the accepted-set error can substantially exceed α. The abstract's claim that SCOPE 'consistently satisfies the target risk bound' conflates the marginal guarantee with per-run validity, and there is no high-probability (e.g., finite-sample binomial-style) control, which is what Clopper–Pearson/ToE baselines actually provide.

The 'FDR' terminology is a misnomer. Eq. 1 is a selection-conditioned error rate defined as a ratio of expectations (P(ŷ≠y*|s≤λ)), which is neither the standard FDR (E[V/max(R,1)]) nor a realized false discovery proportion. Calling it FDR invites confusion with multiple-testing literature and could mislead users about the nature of the guarantee.

The 'bias-neutral' characterization of BPE is asserted, not established. Averaging forward and reverse preference probabilities does not provably remove position bias (a multiplicative position bias would not cancel under averaging), and there is no formal or targeted empirical analysis (e.g., bias decomposition) supporting the claim; the mitigation is only implicit in improved AUROC/ECE.

Guarantee strength depends heavily on the quality of the uncertainty score, and the guarantee itself holds for any score under exchangeability—so the central empirical burden is BPE's ranking quality. Here the margins over the strongest baseline are often small (e.g., AUROC 0.744 vs 0.717 for Llama-70B on MT-Bench, 0.736 vs 0.720 on Chatbot Arena), and coverage remains low in the strictest regimes (e.g., 0.018–0.246 at α=0.05–0.10 for Qwen-7B on MT-Bench), limiting practical impact in the cases where guarantees matter most.

No code release is mentioned; given that the entire evaluation rests on precise logit extraction, prompt templates, and 1,000-split resampling protocols, reproducibility currently depends on the appendix description alone.

Some comparisons are restricted in ways that weaken coverage of the claims (Simulated Annotators and Self-Consistency only on smaller judges; ToE only on MT-Bench), and correctness is measured against human labels that are themselves noisy—only partially addressed by the Appendix F noise experiment on the calibration side.
